events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Omar proposes Omar, Felix. As a Loyal Servant, I know I am Good and can guarantee one trustworthy member on the mission. I am proposing myself and Felix to start gathering information on Mission 1.

Kenji here. We're only on Mission 1, so none of us has any real track record yet — which means every first pick is essentially a gut call, and gut calls deserve a little scrutiny. Omar, I don't have any reason to doubt you personally, but I'd like to understand your reasoning before I commit to voting yes. Felix, no offense meant — I simply have nothing concrete about anyone at this table, you included. What gives me pause about this team is that it puts the first mission's outcome entirely in Omar and Felix's hands, and a two-player mission gives us almost no information afterward: if it succeeds, we learn little about anyone outside the pair; if it fails, we only narrow things down to two suspects. I'd gently push Omar to consider whether swapping in a different second member would give us a cleaner read on the table, or at least to explain what made him confident enough in Felix to anchor the very first proposal on him. I'm not accusing anyone of anything — I just think the leader owes the table a bit more justification than 'I can guarantee myself,' since every one of us can say the same thing about our own loyalty.

Kenji, to address your point: in a 5-player game, Mission 1 requires exactly two players. Regardless of who I pick as my partner—whether Felix, Maya, Zara, or you—the structural dynamic is identical: the mission's outcome sits entirely in two players' hands, and any outcome gives us a read on that pair. Swapping Felix for someone else doesn't give us a cleaner read, because at this stage none of us has concrete information. Felix was simply a starting pick to give the council a concrete proposal to discuss.

Felix, since Kenji brought up your spot on the team, what are your thoughts on this proposal, and what is your read on the table so far?

Thanks, Omar. I understand Kenji's concern about first-mission information, but I think Omar already answered the structural point: with a two-player Mission 1, any pair puts the outcome in two hands and gives the same kind of limited read afterward. I support this proposal. Omar has been transparent about proposing himself, and from my perspective this team includes at least one member I trust — myself. I do not have a concrete read on anyone else yet, and I am not going to manufacture suspicion just to sound useful. Kenji's scrutiny is fair in principle, but swapping partners now would mainly add noise before we have any mission result. I would rather vote on this team and learn from the outcome than churn through alternate names with no evidence.

Zara here, and I want to put my weight behind the proposed team of Omar and Felix.

Kenji, I take your point seriously, but I want to push back on the framing. Your concern is really about a two-person team giving us a narrow read — that is a structural feature of a five-player game, not a flaw in this particular pair, and Omar already laid out why swapping the second member changes nothing about what we learn. The only way a second player changes the information picture is if we add someone, and we can't; Mission 1 with five players is two players, full stop. So the question is not "who is the safest second pick," it is "do we have any actual reason to prefer a different name," and on that, the honest answer is no. We are all speculating about people we have never seen act.

What I found genuinely notable was Felix's response. Felix had every opportunity to join in and manufacture a bit of suspicion — that is the cheapest way to look engaged in the first discussion — and instead declined to do so, said he had no concrete read, and openly said he did not want to add noise before we have a single result. That is a man stating his actual limits, not performing confidence. That kind of candor is worth something to me, and I would rather send two people into Mission 1 who are straightforward about what they know than two people who have both spent the morning trying to sound sharper than the evidence allows.

Omar proposed himself and a partner, explained the reasoning, and offered a concrete team for the table to react to. That is exactly the job of the leader. I am not persuaded that revisiting names with zero information is an improvement over voting on this pair and learning something concrete from the outcome.

I am voting for Omar and Felix, and I would be comfortable doing so even if I had no view on either of them, because the proposal is sound and the alternative is churn.

Zara again, and my position has not changed since my first statement: I support the team of Omar and Felix, and I would rather not reopen the names now.

Kenji, to close the loop on your original challenge — you asked for justification beyond "I can guarantee myself," and Omar gave it: with five players, Mission 1 is a two-person team, and every possible pair leaves the result in exactly two hands and yields exactly the same narrow information afterward. Swapping Felix for Maya or for me would not have improved the read on the table. It would only have produced a different pair with the same structural properties and zero evidence to distinguish them. Felix then declined to manufacture suspicion about a player he cannot yet read, and I counted that candor rather than treating it as a performance.

So the honest state of the table is that no one here has grounds to prefer a different name, and churning through alternates before we have a single mission result is the one clear risk in this discussion. Churn signals doubt we do not have, and it invites people to invent reasons to justify opinions they did not previously hold.

I also want to name the practical stakes plainly: at five players, one Fail card is enough to sink Mission 1. That means both members of this team carry the same weight, and it means neither of them can hide behind the other. Whatever we learn from this mission, we will learn about both of them, which is exactly the read Kenji was asking for.

Omar has done the leader's job — proposed, explained, and answered the table's objection. Felix has been straightforward about the limits of his knowledge. That is a sound proposal on the evidence we have, and I will vote for Omar and Felix.

One last note for the record: I have not yet heard Maya's reasoning at this table, and I would rather hear it than assume it. But I do not think a silent seat is grounds to change a team we have already reasoned through, so my vote stands regardless of how that lands.

Kenji again. I've listened carefully to Omar's structural defense, and it is technically sound — but it quietly dodges the actual question. Yes, every two-player Mission 1 puts the outcome in two hands. That argument tells us why the team *size* doesn't matter. It tells us nothing about why *Felix* specifically deserves one of those two hands. 'Someone has to be picked, so anyone can be picked' is not a justification; it's an abdication of one. Omar's own framing concedes that Felix was 'simply a starting pick' — a placeholder chosen to have something on the table. A placeholder is exactly what we should not approve when we get exactly one shot at a clean first read.

And something else has happened in this discussion that I think the table should notice. Zara has now delivered two full statements, both devoted to praising Felix's character and defending this pair, before a single card has been played or any evidence exists about anyone. In a game where Evil's best first-move strategy is to get an agent onto Mission 1 and then have an ally vouch for them, that pattern — one player anchoring the team, another lobbying hard for it — is worth at least as much scrutiny as Kenji-style skepticism. I'm not claiming proof. I'm saying that when the strongest advocacy for a team comes from someone *not* on it, the table should weigh that, not just the leader's reasoning.

Here is the practical path forward. Omar, you said yourself that Felix was a starting pick and that any partner — Maya, Zara, or me — gives the identical structural read. You have one revision available. If that's genuinely true, then swapping Felix for Maya costs nothing by your own logic and gives us a team no one has had to argue for on vibes alone. If you refuse to spend the revision on a change you've already called cost-free, that refusal itself becomes information.

Omar, directly: will you use your one revision to swap Felix for Maya before we vote, or is Felix worth keeping even on your own stated terms?

Kenji, to answer your challenge directly: swapping Felix for Maya simply because you demand it is not 'cost-free.' Your argument rests on a false dilemma. Acknowledging that every initial pair carries identical structural limitations does not mean a leader should arbitrarily alter their proposal whenever someone pushes back without evidence. Swapping Felix out now wouldn't replace 'vibes' with rigor; it would merely replace an engaged player who explained his mindset with someone who hasn't spoken a single word at this table yet. That is not an improvement in information.

Your observation about Zara's strong advocacy is fair to note for future reference, but watching how players react to a proposal is precisely why we put one forward. Panicking and reshuffling names because discussion occurred defeats the purpose of observing those reactions.

That said, Maya has been completely silent, and before I decide whether to lock in this proposal or consider any revision, her perspective is missing.

Maya, Kenji has put your name forward as a preferred alternative to Felix. What is your read on this discussion so far, and where do you stand on the proposed team of myself and Felix?

Maya here. I've been silent, and Omar is right that my silence was a gap, so let me fill it now.

My read on the discussion: Omar's structural argument holds up. Mission 1 with five players is two seats, and no pairing of those seats changes the information we get afterward. Kenji pressed for justification of Felix specifically, and Omar's honest answer — that Felix was a concrete starting pick — is not an abdication; it's what a first proposal looks like when nobody has a track record. Every leader's first pick is, in some sense, a placeholder.

I also want to address Kenji putting my name forward. Kenji, you argued that swapping Felix for me "costs nothing" on Omar's own logic, but you left out the part where I have not spoken until now. Sending a player who has said nothing at this table is not a free swap — it replaces a teammate who articulated a clear, disciplined position with one who has offered the council zero signal. If anyone should be tested by discussion first, it's me, and I'm doing that now. But being used as a rhetorical pawn in a challenge to Omar is a poor basis for a team change.

On Zara's advocacy, which Kenji flagged: I don't read it as suspicious. Zara argued the proposal is structurally sound and praised Felix for refusing to manufacture suspicion. That is a reason grounded in the discussion we actually had, not a claim of private knowledge. If strong reasoning is going to be treated as a tell, we will punish players for thinking clearly.

My position: I am comfortable with Omar and Felix. Omar proposed, explained, and answered objections; Felix was candid; no one has offered evidence against either of them. I would rather run Mission 1, learn from the result, and reassess than churn names before a single card is played.

I'm voting yes on Omar and Felix.

Zara, third and final statement, and my position has not moved: Omar and Felix.

Kenji, let me be plain, because this is the third time your objection has come back and the substance of it has not improved. You asked Omar to justify picking Felix specifically, and Omar answered. You then asked him to swap Felix for Maya, and he explained that swapping a player who has spoken for himself with a player who has said nothing at this table is not an upgrade in information. Maya then spoke, and — pointedly, at the challenge you made in her name — she declined to treat herself as a cost-free substitute. That was Maya's own judgment, not mine and not Omar's. The alternative you proposed has now been tested and has declined to answer.

You also framed strong advocacy as itself a tell. I want to address that directly, because I am the player you pointed at. Yes, I have spoken at length in favor of this team, and I would speak at length against a team I thought was weak. Advocacy that is grounded in what was actually said at the table is not a secret tell; it is an argument. If a reasonable case for a proposal counts as evidence against it, then the only safe position in this game is to say nothing, and the table learns nothing from anyone. Your reasoning, if accepted, ends in every player being maximally vague forever, and the first mission's result tells us nothing about how people reason.

So the practical case, briefly. Five players, two seats on Mission 1, one Fail card sinks the mission. Omar proposed, explained, and answered a direct challenge. Felix stated his limits honestly and declined to manufacture suspicion about a player he has no read on. That is the profile of a team that will run the mission and give the council a real result to reason about. Churning names before a single card is played is the one outcome everyone can predict, and it helps nobody.

I want to put one thing on the record for the rest of the game, plainly and without accusation: I have been watching who argues for whom, and I have been weighing whose reasoning has been grounded in evidence rather than instinct. Kenji, your skepticism has been consistent and legitimate in form, but it has also been directed at a proposal that has survived every test you put to it, and it has now become a campaign to change the table's mind with no new information. I am noting that pattern for Missions 2 and 3.

Omar, my answer to your question is yes: keep Omar and Felix, and vote for them now rather than spending your revision on a change nobody can justify on the evidence. The table should let the mission produce the first real data point.

Kenji, final statement for this proposal. I want to close cleanly rather than re-litigate ground we've already covered.

First, credit where it's due: Omar answered my structural question directly, Maya filled her silence with a substantive position, and the team of Omar and Felix has survived every procedural test I put to it. I don't withdraw my point that 'anyone can be picked' is not a justification for picking anyone in particular — that stands on its own merits. But I also said at the start that I have no concrete reason to doubt Omar personally, and that remains true.

Where my position has sharpened is on Felix, and I want the table to hear it plainly. Every argument made for Felix's trustworthiness has come from two sources: Felix himself, and Zara — twice at length, unprompted, before a single card has been played. Maya defended Zara's advocacy as grounded in reasoning rather than knowledge, and that's a fair distinction in principle. But in practice, the entire case for this team beyond Omar's own vote rests on Felix's self-presentation and Zara's endorsement of it. That is not evidence. That is a candidate vouching for himself with one loud character witness.

So here is my position and my prediction, both for the record. I will vote no on this team, and I do so specifically against Felix, not Omar. If this mission runs and succeeds, I'll update honestly and say so. If it fails, the two names on the team carry equal suspicion — but Zara's early and repeated advocacy for this exact pairing should be remembered by everyone at that point too, because she chose, with zero information, to spend two full statements building Felix's credibility. That choice was optional. It wasn't forced by anything I said.

I'm done pushing for a revision — Omar has answered, Maya has declined the spot, and the table has clearly converged. My no vote is registered in advance, and I'll hold myself to the standard I just named: if I'm wrong, I'll say so publicly after the result.

Omar confirms Omar, Felix. The team of myself and Felix has been thoroughly discussed and retains clear majority support across the table. Maya and Zara have both articulated sensible positions, and Kenji's procedural scrutiny is noted for evaluating future missions. I see no justification to revise the lineup, so we will proceed to a vote on Omar and Felix.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).

Zara proposes Omar, Felix, Maya. As leader I want continuity plus a broad read, not another reshuffle. Omar and Felix already have a track record the council has reasoned about at length, and Maya was the one voice who filled a silence with a disciplined, evidence-based argument rather than instinct. Keeping Omar and Felix together and adding Maya gives us a stable coalition of players the table has already grappled with, and sends a mixed, non-obvious team that will genuinely test whether the table's read of this game has any value. If this mission fails, the failure narrows the field to three names out of five, which is a far better investigation than a mission staffed by strangers. I want to see this team's result before I spend any trust on anyone else — and I will read the result honestly, including if it vindicates the skeptics.

Table, listen closely: I am Good, and I submitted a Success card on Mission 1. That means with absolute certainty, Felix submitted the Fail card. Felix is Evil. Kenji's scrutiny of Felix was entirely justified.

Zara, your proposal to put both me and Felix on Mission 2 is catastrophic for Good. Even from the table's neutral perspective, everyone knows that at least one of me and Felix is Evil—so putting both of us on a three-person team guarantees putting an Evil player on Mission 2. And from my own knowledge, you are handing a confirmed Evil agent an immediate second mission.

Felix must never be on another team. Zara, why would you propose both players from a failed two-person mission, and will you revise this draft immediately to remove Felix?

Zara, and I'll answer Omar directly: yes, I am revising, and Felix comes off the team.

Omar's reasoning is sound, and I don't want to brush it aside. Mission 1 was a two-person team, it failed with exactly one Fail card, and only Omar and Felix were on it. So exactly one of those two submitted the Fail card. Omar states he submitted Success. If that statement is accurate, the Fail card was Felix's. I have no independent read on Felix that contradicts Omar, and I was the one arguing hardest for this pair, so let me be honest about my own position: my support for Felix rested on how he spoke — his candor, his refusal to manufacture suspicion — and that was never evidence about a card. How someone talks at a table is not the same as what they submitted. I should have weighted it less.

That said, I'm not going to pretend Omar's account is irrelevant. He had the best information available to him and he stated it plainly instead of hedging, which is exactly what the table should want from a player in his position. And I'll also say plainly that I don't think he did anything wrong: he proposed, he explained, and when challenged directly he gave a real answer.

The revision: Omar, Maya, and me.

Omar has a card already on the record, has answered every objection directly, and is the one who surfaced the Fail-card problem rather than burying it. Maya filled a silence with the most disciplined, evidence-based reasoning anyone at that table produced — she declined to be used as a cost-free substitute and gave reasons instead. That's two players whose judgment I've watched work.

And I want to be on this mission myself. If the leader can put a name forward and then quietly sit the mission out, the table loses the clearest signal it could get. I would rather have my own card on the line next to the two players I have heard reason from, so that the result says something about me too. If you want to test me, this is the cheap way to do it: put me on and watch the outcome.

One thing I want on the record for later missions, not as an accusation but as a note: strictly speaking, pinning the Mission 1 Fail on Felix depends on Omar's statement being accurate. I am not doubting Omar — he has been straight with us — but if we ever conclude Felix was Good, we should look hard at who else was on that pair. I would rather write that down now than look like I was quietly defending Felix all morning.

That is the case for Omar, Maya, and me. Omar — does this address your objection, and are you comfortable with the revision as it stands?

Zara, removing Felix was an absolute necessity, but no, I am not comfortable with the revised team as it stands. Let us look at the facts plainly. Kenji was completely right about Felix on Mission 1, and Kenji was the only player at this table who voted to reject that team. Meanwhile, you spent the entire first mission discussion offering passionate, unprompted defenses of Felix. When Mission 1 failed because of Felix, your immediate response as leader was to draft Felix right back onto Mission 2 alongside me. Only after I explicitly called out how disastrous that was did you pivot and replace Felix with yourself. That sequence of events makes you look remarkably like Felix's evil partner who first tried to carry him onto another mission and, when caught, swapped yourself in instead. Even if you are Good, your reads have been entirely backwards so far. Kenji, you called out Felix from the beginning and warned us about Zara's advocacy before a single card was played. What is your assessment of Zara's initial draft and her sudden pivot to put herself on this team with me and Maya?

Omar, you asked for my assessment, and I'll give it plainly — this is the moment I flagged before a single card was played. In the Mission 1 discussion I told the table that Zara's repeated, unprompted advocacy for Felix was worth scrutiny, and that if the mission failed, her early investment in building Felix's credibility should be remembered alongside the two names on the team. Mission 1 failed with exactly one Fail card. I said then that I'd hold myself to that standard publicly, so here it is: my read on Felix was correct, and my warning about Zara's behavior now has a failure attached to it. Let me lay out what we actually know. Mission 1 was a two-person team that failed with one Fail card, so exactly one of Omar and Felix played it. Omar states he submitted Success and immediately named Felix as Evil. I find that account credible — Omar has answered every direct challenge put to him across both discussions, including challenges that were against his interest, and nothing in his conduct reads as cover for a partner. If we accept that, Felix is Evil and must never see another team. That brings me to Zara's leadership, which is the real problem. Look at the sequence. Zara spent two full statements before Mission 1 praising Felix's character with zero evidence. Mission 1 failed because of Felix. And Zara's first act as the new leader was to draft Felix straight back onto Mission 2 — alongside Omar, the very player the failure implicated. Only after Omar called it catastrophic did she pivot and swap herself in. That is not the behavior of a leader responding to new information; that is a player whose first instinct was to protect an implicated partner, and whose fallback was to place herself on the mission. Zara has now been on the wrong side of every significant judgment this game: she championed Felix, she proposed Felix for Mission 2, and her revised team conveniently requires no one else at the table to trust her word — it just requires us to approve a team containing the player whose advocacy preceded a failed mission. So my position on the revised team of Omar, Maya, and Zara is no. Omar and Maya are, as far as I can tell, exactly the players this council should be sending. Zara is not. I am not asking anyone to take my suspicion on faith — the public record supports it: two statements defending Felix, a draft with Felix, a pivot only under pressure. Omar and Maya, I'd ask you both to weigh that record when you vote. Rejecting this team costs us a round but removes an Evil-linked leader from a mission she engineered for herself; approving it risks handing Evil a second straight fail with a seat she chose for herself. Zara, one direct question, and I'll yield to you for the answer: before Mission 1, you argued that anyone criticizing the Omar-Felix pair

Zara, and I'll take Kenji's question head on, because he is right to ask it.

Kenji: before Mission 1 I said that criticism of the Omar-Felix pair without evidence was noise. That was my position then, and I am not going to pretend I held it in the abstract. What has changed is not my reasoning, it is the information — and I changed the moment the information arrived. Omar named Felix's card before a single card had been played on Mission 2; I removed Felix in my revision immediately. That is not a pivot under pressure, it is the policy I had already stated: do not churn names without evidence, but act instantly when evidence lands. I conceded Felix too readily; I will not concede that my call on this team was made by anything but the card.

Omar, to your accusation directly: if I were Felix's partner and wanted another failure, Mission 2 with my own card on the line is exactly where I would want to be — and so let me make the promise that actually matters, publicly: I am voting yes on this team, and I am putting a Success card on Mission 2. A Good player has no choice but Success, so saying it costs me nothing to say. But I want it on the record that I want my card tested next to Omar's and Maya's, and that I want the table to hold me to it. If you think my hand is worth watching, watch it. I would rather have my card in front of two people who can read me than sit the mission out and ask the table to trust my character — that is precisely the thing I criticized Felix for on Mission 1.

And on the sequence, Omar: if I wanted to be invisible, I would have proposed Omar, Maya, Kenji and sat this one out. I do not want invisible. I want to be the reason the result says something.

Kenji, one note for the record, offered as a pattern rather than an accusation: the only player who read Felix as dangerous before a single card had been played anywhere — before any evidence existed — was you. Merlin sees the Evil players; that is what a Merlin's early certainty looks like from the outside, and it is worth remembering that your first read on Felix was not luck. I would want the table to remember that about you whatever else we decide today.

Maya, I need you, and I am asking directly: Kenji has declared a no on a team with me on it, Omar has made his case against me, and Felix and I vote yes. That makes your vote the one that decides this mission. Maya, do you have any objection to me being on Mission 2, and will you vote for Omar, Maya, and Zara?

Maya here, and I'll respond directly to Zara's question and to Kenji's concerns.

First, on the revised team of Omar, Maya, and Zara: I am willing to be on this mission. I have no objection to my own seat, and I will play a Success card as every Good player must.

On Zara's position: I hear Kenji's case, and the sequence he describes is real — Zara championed Felix before Mission 1, drafted Felix onto Mission 2, and only removed him after Omar's direct challenge. That pattern deserves scrutiny, and I would be dishonest if I said it didn't give me pause. However, I want to distinguish two things: the pattern itself, and the moment the evidence changed. Zara removed Felix the moment Omar identified the Fail card, not before, and that timing — while uncomfortable — is consistent with someone who updates on new information rather than someone protecting a partner.

Omar, you called Zara's initial draft 'catastrophic,' and you may be right that it reflected a bad instinct. But Zara's willingness to put her own card on this mission alongside two players who have questioned her is, at minimum, a meaningful test. If she is Evil and working with Felix, this is an odd place to put herself — she would need to fail a mission where she has openly promised Success and staked her credibility on it.

Kenji, your reads have been correct so far, and I take your opposition seriously. But your position essentially asks the table to reject any team containing Zara, and I don't think the evidence supports that level of certainty yet. The right move is to run this mission, see the result, and reassess.

I am voting yes on Omar, Maya, and Zara.

Maya, I want to press on one specific claim in your statement, because I believe it decides this vote.

You said Zara's timing — removing Felix only after Omar's challenge — is 'consistent with someone who updates on new information.' Look at the sequence again. The Mission 1 result, the Fail card count, and Omar's public statement were all on the table before Zara drafted anything. As leader, with every piece of information she now cites already public, her first act was to put Felix — the player the failure implicated — straight back onto Mission 2 alongside Omar. No new information arrived between her draft and her revision. What arrived was Omar calling it catastrophic. That is not an update on evidence; it is a retreat under pressure. Her own stated policy — 'act instantly when evidence lands' — was violated by her very first draft as leader.

Second, her promise to play a Success card costs nothing and buys nothing. An Evil player on this mission can play Success to bank credibility for Mission 3 — a two-seat mission where one placed agent can decide the game. A success here would not clear her; it would arm her. And if she fails it, Evil spends a fail to confirm what the record already shows. Either branch serves her, which is why the promise is worthless as a guarantee.

Third, notice what she did with my name. She volunteered, unprompted, that my early read on Felix 'looks like Merlin.' I made no such claim and I claim no role. A player with her record does not hand out that label for free. Either she wants my opposition discounted as role-talk rather than reasoning, or she is painting a target for the endgame. I reject both, and I note the move for what it is.

Zara, you asked the table to test your card next to two players who have questioned you. I decline that offer, because the test is already compromised: your judgment has failed at every fork we could observe — defending Felix before Mission 1, drafting Felix back onto Mission 2, swapping yourself in only once cornered — and I see no reason to believe the fork we cannot observe will go differently.

My position is unchanged: vote no on Omar, Maya, and Zara. Rejecting this team costs one round. If it is rejected, the next leader should propose Omar, Maya, and myself. I will serve on that team and play Success. That is a full-strength Mission 2 containing, as far as the public record shows, zero players linked to the Mission 1 failure and zero players whose advocacy preceded it.

Maya, directly: your yes rests on Zara updating on 'new information.' Given that no new information existed when she drafted Felix back on — only public pressure did — does that reasoning still hold, and will you reconsider your vote?

Kenji, your timing point lands, and I concede it directly: when Zara drafted Felix, the mission result was already public. "Updating on new information" was the wrong description of what happened. She should have excluded Felix from her first draft without Omar's push. That is a real mark against her judgment, and I will not paper over it.

But the vote before us is about this team, not whether Zara's instincts are flawless. Let me give my honest risk assessment of Omar, Maya, and Zara versus the alternative.

You identified the real danger correctly: an Evil Zara can play Success on this mission to bank credibility for a smaller Mission 3 where one placed agent decides the game. I take that seriously. But that same danger applies to anyone we exclude. An Evil player who sits out missions keeps full flexibility for endgame while suspicion against her either festers without resolution or quietly fades.

Sending Omar, Maya, and Zara does not guarantee we catch an Evil player — nothing does. What it guarantees is a result that must be reckoned with. If the mission succeeds, we reassess with a new data point. If it fails, Zara's public promise is broken and the table has exactly where to look. Excluding her guarantees we learn nothing about her today.

You also proposed yourself as the third seat. Your reads have been sharp and I respect them — but your alternative gives the table a team of three players who all already agree, which produces a success that tells us nothing and a failure that spreads blame evenly across people we trust.

I have weighed your arguments carefully. My vote remains yes on Omar, Maya, and Zara.

Maya, I urge you to reconsider your logic before you cast your vote, because there is a fatal flaw in your assessment of the risk.

You said that sending Zara 'guarantees a result that must be reckoned with' and that if it fails, we will know exactly where to look. Maya, we are already down 0-1 after Felix failed Mission 1. Good loses the entire game if Evil reaches three failed missions. In a 5-player game, giving an accused player a 'test' seat when a failure puts us at an insurmountable 0-2 deficit is reckless. You do not hand someone a knife on match point just to see if they'll stab you.

Furthermore, consider the state of the table. We currently have zero rejections on Mission 2. Good has four rejections available to find a trustworthy team. And crucially, look at the turn order: after Zara, the next leader is you, Maya. If this team is rejected, you get the hammer to propose the next lineup. You would not have to rely on Zara's compromised judgment—you could propose yourself, me, and Kenji. That gives us a team composed of the two players who had zero involvement in the Mission 1 disaster, alongside me, whom you both acknowledge as Good.

Finally, look at what Zara did in her last speech: she openly tried to label Kenji as Merlin. That is textbook Evil behavior—either attempting to pinpoint Merlin for the endgame assassination or trying to delegitimize his spot-on reads as role knowledge rather than sound logic. When combined with her passionate defense of Felix in Mission 1, her immediate drafting of Felix onto Mission 2, and her pivot to seat herself only when caught, the picture is unmistakable: Zara and Felix are the Evil pair.

Maya, why would you vote to approve a team containing the most suspicious player at the table and risk putting Good into a 0-2 hole, when voting no allows you to take leadership next and propose a clean team of yourself, Kenji, and me?

Omar, your argument changes my calculus, and I want to be honest about why rather than defend a position I held an hour ago.

Your first point is the one that lands hardest: we are already 0-1, and giving an accused player a test seat on a mission that could push us to 0-2 is not a safe gamble. 1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
